FSSAI issues notices to Nestle, Zydus Wellness over ‘misleading claims’ in Complan, Lactogen, Nan
Edited by
Vriti Jain

The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India has issued notices regarding misleading claims by Nestle and Zydus Wellness.
NEW DELHI: The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) on Wednesday issued notices to Nestle India and Zydus Wellness over alleged misleading claims and non-compliant promotions in products including Complan, Lactogen Pro 1 Powder and Nan Excella Pro Stage 1.
The regulator has asked the companies to provide scientific evidence to substantiate the claims made in their product labels and advertisements.
In a social media post, FSSAI said it had issued notices to Nestle India over claims made for Lactogen Pro 1 Powder and Nan Excella Pro Stage 1, and to Zydus Wellness Products Ltd over advertisements for Complan.
FSSAI questioned the claim that Lactogen Pro 1 Powder contains whey protein, described in its labelling and advertising as a milk protein that is easy to digest.
The regulator has asked Nestle India to provide scientific evidence supporting the claim.
For Nan Excella Pro Stage 1, FSSAI flagged the claim that “5 HMOs help support the normal immune system”, saying it could imply that the product is suitable for supporting the immune system.
The regulator said the claim was considered non-compliant with provisions restricting claims relating to the prevention, alleviation, treatment or cure of diseases and certain physiological conditions, unless specifically permitted under applicable regulations.
FSSAI also sought scientific substantiation for the product's claim that it contains whey protein. Nestle India has been directed to explain why action should not be initiated against it under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006.
A Nestle India spokesperson said, “FSSAI’s recent post reiterates the points raised in its earlier post of September 18 regarding product labels. We have already submitted our detailed response to FSSAI on these matters.”
For Zydus Wellness' Complan, the regulator flagged claims including “2X Faster Growth”, “Supports Concentration and Memory” and “Pro Immunity+ 34 Vital Nutrients”, displayed alongside images of two children on the product label.
FSSAI said the claims violated the Food Safety and Standards (Advertising and Claims) Regulations, 2018. It also flagged the advertisement claim “growth comes in 4 flavors” as violating the regulations.
The regulator has directed Zydus Wellness to provide scientific justification for the claims and show cause within the stipulated period as to why action should not be taken against the company.
(With agency inputs)

Priyagold biscuits ban: Why did Nepal ban popular Indian cookies after FSSAI crackdown? What is the main issue?
Nepal has banned Priyagold biscuits made by India's Surya Food and Agro after FSSAI alleged cattle feed bran use and serious food safety violations.

Nepal has banned Priyagold biscuits made by India's Surya Food and Agro after FSSAI flagged alleged use of cattle feed bran and serious food safety violations. (AI generated image)
AI Quick Read
Nepal has banned the import, sale and distribution of Priyagold biscuits manufactured by India's Surya Food and Agro Ltd, citing food safety concerns after India's food regulator initiated legal proceedings against the company over alleged violations, including the use of cattle feed bran in biscuit production.
The Food Technology and Quality Control Department (FTQCD) announced the restrictions in a notice issued on Monday, describing the biscuits as sub-standard,
PTI
reported. The decision follows action by the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI), which has also suspended the manufacturer's licence.
Why has Nepal banned Priyagold biscuits?
Nepal's decision is linked to food safety concerns raised by India's FSSAI following an inspection of Surya Food and Agro, the manufacturer of Priyagold biscuits.

|
FSSAI prosecutes Surya Food for using cattle feed bran in Priyagold biscuits
According to the Indian regulator, the inspection revealed serious deficiencies in food safety and hygiene. FSSAI has initiated legal proceedings for prosecution against the company over the alleged use of cattle feed bran in manufacturing Priyagold biscuits, along with other serious violations.
The Nepalese department cited the notice published by FSSAI as the basis for its decision to prohibit the biscuits' import and sale,
PTI
reported. The suspension of the manufacturer's licence in India was also part of the regulatory action surrounding the product.
The Nepalese authorities have not announced a separate inspection finding in the information provided. Their stated rationale for the ban rests on the food safety concerns and regulatory action reported by India's food regulator.
What action has Nepal taken against Priyagold biscuits?
The FTQCD imposed restrictions on the import, sale and distribution of
Priyagold biscuits manufactured in India
. The move was approved following an emergency meeting convened virtually at the initiative of the department's director general, Sanjeev Kumar Karna.
The notice said the decision was taken with human health security and consumer welfare in mind.
Also Read
|
FSSAI proposes ban on added sugar in baby food for infants aged up to six months
The Nepalese department has directed traders, relevant organisations and consumers not to import the biscuits and has called for sales and distribution to stop. Authorised importers and food traders have also been instructed to recall existing stocks from the market immediately.
What is the main issue in the Priyagold biscuits case?
The central issue is the alleged use of cattle feed bran in the manufacture of biscuits intended for human consumption, alongside other food safety and hygiene deficiencies identified during the Indian regulator's inspection.
Cattle feed bran is a by-product used in animal feed. Its alleged use in biscuit production has prompted regulatory scrutiny, although the allegations should be distinguished from a final determination of liability
Also Read
|
FSSAI warns nutraceutical firms over labelling violations, threatens action
FSSAI's legal proceedings against Surya Food and Agro
indicate that the matter has moved beyond routine inspection findings. The suspension of the company's licence represents a further regulatory step, while Nepal's ban extends the consequences of the case to the Indian manufacturer's access to the Nepalese market.
The available notice does not specify the quantity of biscuits affected, the number of retail outlets involved or whether any illnesses have been linked to consumption of the product.
What should importers and consumers in Nepal do?
The Nepalese food regulator has asked authorised importers and food traders to withdraw any available stocks of Priyagold biscuits from the market. It has also urged consumers and other concerned parties to refrain from importing, selling or distributing the product.
The restrictions follow the food safety concerns raised by India's regulator and the suspension of Surya Food and Agro's licence. Further action will depend on the regulatory process and any subsequent directions issued by the authorities.
For now, the ban prevents the affected Priyagold biscuits from being imported or sold in Nepal, as officials seek to protect consumers amid allegations of serious manufacturing violations.

In an exclusive interview with NDTV Food, Maharashtra Food Chief Tukaram Mundhe explains how the authority traces adulterated products through the supply chain and takes action to prevent further exposure.

Tukaram Mundhe is being lauded for his food safety crackdowns.
Show
Quick Read
Summary is AI-generated, newsroom-reviewed
Maharashtra FDA Chief Tukaram Mundhe explains how adulterated food is traced back to its source
The department traces adulterated food from retailer to raw-material supplier using records
Mundhe shared a step-by-step process that the authority undertakes for tracking
How do investigators prove if food adulteration was done on purpose?
When an adulterated food product is found on a shop shelf, removing it from sale is only the first step. The danger is not over; the problem is not solved. The bigger challenge is finding out where it came from, how it reached the market and whether the same batch has been supplied to other retailers.
In an exclusive interaction with NDTV Food, Maharashtra Food and Drug Administration (FDA) Commissioner Tukaram Mundhe explains how they follow an evidence-led process to trace adulterated food products, establish accountability and take action against those responsible. This requires tracing the product through every link in the supply chain, from the retailer and distributor to the manufacturer and raw-material supplier.
READ
|
Exclusive: India's Food Safety Problem Goes Beyond Just Dirty Kitchens - By Tukaram Mundhe
How Does the FDA Trace Adulterated Products To Its Source? Tukaram Mundhe Explains
In Maharashtra, the Food and Drug Administration follows a structured, evidence-led process to move from the shop shelf to the source.
Step 1: Start With The Product
The label carries the manufacturer's name, the batch or lot number, the date of manufacture and the FSSAI licence number. A check on FoSCoS tells us who holds the licence, where the unit is located and which authority licensed it.
Step 2: Follow The Records
Every licensed food business must keep purchase and sale records. Our Food Safety Officers examine:
(i) The retailer's purchase invoice, which leads to the distributor or wholesaler;
(ii) The distributor's records, which lead to the manufacturer or packer;
(iii) The manufacturer's raw-material, production and dispatch records, which show both where the inputs came from and where else the same batch was sent.
Step 3: Sample And Analyse
Samples are drawn under the statutory procedure and sent to accredited laboratories. Analysis tells us whether the food is unsafe, substandard or misbranded, which determines the action to follow. Nationally, 31,407 legal cases were launched in 2024-25 on the basis of non-conforming samples.
Step 4: Contain The Risk
(i) Suspect stock can be seized under Section 38 of the Food Safety and Standards Act.
(ii) The food business operator is responsible for recalling unsafe food from the market under Section 28 of the Act and the FSS (Food Recall Procedure) Regulations, 2017.
(iii) Licences can be suspended where the risk demands it.
Step 5: Fix Liability Along The Chain
Section 27 of the Act sets out the responsibilities of manufacturers, distributors and retailers. A retailer who can show a valid warranty from his supplier passes responsibility up the chain. This is why records matter so much for honest traders.
Step 6: Coordinate Beyond Our Boundaries
Where the chain crosses district or state borders, we refer the matter to the Designated Officer or Food Safety Commissioner concerned, and to FSSAI for centrally licensed units and imported food.
Step 7: Involve The Police In Organised Adulteration
Where there is evidence of deliberate, organised adulteration, we work with the police. Criminal provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita on adulteration of food and sale of noxious food apply alongside the Food Safety and Standards Act. This allows us to investigate the entire network, including financiers, chemical suppliers and transporters.
READ
|
Exclusive: Tukaram Mundhe On Why Cheap Food Can Come At A Higher Cost
Tukaram Mundhe explains how they follow an evidence-led process to trace adulterated food products
The Objective Is To Trace The Source, Not Just Remove The Product
Tracing adulterated food requires more than identifying a product that fails a quality test. The investigation must establish where the product originated, how it moved through the supply chain and who was responsible at each stage. Purchase invoices, manufacturing records, batch numbers and laboratory reports help investigators build that chain of evidence.

efet_title: FSSAI mulls stricter regulations for baby food, proposes ban on added sugar | India News - Hindustan Times
efet_body:
FSSAI mulls stricter regulations for baby food, proposes ban on added sugar
The ministry of health and family welfare said the emphasis is on minimising exposure to added sugars during the earliest stages of life.
Published on: Oct 17, 2026, 19:15:58 IST
Edited by
Anushka Awasthi
Prefer HT
on Google
Share via
Copy link
The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) has proposed banning the addition of fructose and sucrose in food products for infants up to six months of age, an official statement said on Saturday.
FSSAI focuses on science-based food standards, responsible product formulation and preventive nutrition, the ministry said. (Representative Image/Unsplash)
The aim is to strengthen nutritional safeguards for infants, according to the statement from the ministry of health and family welfare.
Also Read |
FSSAI issues order to intensify food safety crackdown across India ahead of festive season to prevent sale of ‘adulterated, unsafe products’
'Aim to reduce early exposure to added sugars': FSSAI
Sharing the update on X, the FSSAI wrote, "FSSAI proposes strengthening infant nutrition standards by restricting the addition of sucrose and fructose in food products intended for infants up to six months of age."
"The draft amendment aims to reduce early exposure to added sugars," it added.
FSSAI's move for infant nutrition
Food regulator FSSAI has published a draft amendment to the Food Safety and Standards (Foods for Infant Nutrition) Regulations, 2020, proposing to "prohibit the addition of sucrose and fructose in food products intended for infants up to six months of age".
The draft notification has been published for public consultation and the stakeholders can submit objections and suggestions within 60 days.
According to the ministry's statement, the draft Food Safety and Standards (Foods for Infant Nutrition) Amendment Regulations, 2026, seeks to strengthen the existing regulatory framework by ensuring that infant nutrition products are formulated in accordance with age-appropriate nutritional requirements.
The emphasis is on minimising exposure to added sugars during the earliest stages of life, it added.
Currently, the existing regulations prescribe comprehensive nutritional composition, quality and safety standards for various categories of infant nutrition products, for children from birth up to 24 months of age.
"Under the current provisions, lactose and glucose polymers are the preferred sources of carbohydrates, while sucrose and/or fructose may be added only when required as a carbohydrate source, subject to prescribed limits," the statement read.
Now, the draft amendment proposes a specific restriction on the addition of sucrose and fructose in products intended for infants up to six months of age.
Also Read |
FSSAI recalls Everest cumin power over ‘unsafe’ pesticide levels, suspends Creative Bakers' licence
The ministry noted that the proposed provision states that "sucrose and fructose shall not be added in the products intended for infants up to the age of 6 months".
"The first six months of life represent a critical period for healthy growth and development, making appropriate nutrition particularly important. The proposed restriction seeks to ensure that infant nutrition products meet the nutritional needs of this age group without unnecessary addition of sucrose and fructose," the ministry said.
Public health efforts
The move is also intended to support broader public health efforts to address concerns associated with early exposure to added sugars, including dietary risk factors linked to childhood obesity and related health challenges, it further noted.
"The initiative complements established public health recommendations promoting exclusive breastfeeding during the first six months of life," the ministry observed.
The proposed amendment seeks to support appropriate infant feeding practices.
It also encourages manufacturers to adopt formulations that prioritise the specific nutritional requirements of young infants.
Also Read |
'Food handlers with long nails, fungus on veggies': Top Delhi hotel operator gets FSSAI notice
"The proposed regulatory measure reflects FSSAI's continued focus on science-based food standards, responsible product formulation and preventive nutrition," the ministry stated.

efet_body:
View Market Dashboard FSSAI notifies draft amendment to tighten infant nutrition rules: What are the changes being proposed? FSSAI has proposed banning the addition of sucrose and fructose to infant nutrition products for babies up to six months old. The draft amendment is open for public feedback for 60 days before the regulator considers finalising it. Garvit Bhirani Updated 17 Oct 2026, 04:10 PM IST Prefer Livemint on Google FSSAI seeks to tighten infant nutrition rules: What are changes being proposed? (Images: HT, Representational/ Unsplash) AI Quick Read The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) has released a draft amendment to the Food Safety and Standards (Foods for Infant Nutrition) Regulations, 2020, proposing a ban on adding sucrose and fructose to food products meant for infants aged up to six months. Published on Friday, the draft Food Safety and Standards (Foods for Infant Nutrition) Amendment Regulations, 2026, aim to further strengthen nutritional requirements for infant food products by restricting the addition of sugars during the initial months of a child's life, according to ANI . What changes are being proposed? Currently, lactose and glucose polymers are recommended as the primary carbohydrate sources in infant nutrition products. The existing rules, however, allow manufacturers to use sucrose and/or fructose as carbohydrate sources when necessary, provided they adhere to the specified limits. The proposed amendment seeks to remove this allowance for products manufactured for infants up to six months old. Also Read | Blinkit, Instamart and Amazon Now could face stricter FSSAI rules The draft provision states that "sucrose and fructose shall not be added in the products intended for infants up to the age of 6 months". If implemented, the provision would prevent manufacturers from adding either of these sugars to infant nutrition products designed for children in this age group. Why is FSSAI proposing the change? FSSAI has highlighted that the first six months of an infant's life are a crucial phase of growth and development, during which adequate and appropriate nutrition plays a vital role. The proposed measure is intended to ensure that products formulated for young infants fulfil their nutritional requirements without the addition of sucrose and fructose where they are not necessary. Also Read | ‘Milky Mist denies FSSAI inquiry on paneer products’: Here’s what company said The move also supports wider public health initiatives aimed at reducing the risks associated with early exposure to added sugars, including dietary factors contributing to childhood obesity and other related health concerns. How does the proposal align with breastfeeding recommendations? The proposed restrictions are in line with established public health guidance that recommends exclusive breastfeeding for the first six months after birth. Through stricter nutritional requirements for infant food products, the regulator aims to promote formulations that cater to the specific dietary needs of infants during their early months. Also Read | Ayodhya's Ram Mandir to get FSSAI 'Eat Right Place' tag, says report The existing regulations lay down detailed requirements for nutritional composition, quality and safety across different categories of infant nutrition products intended for children from birth to 24 months. What happens next? FSSAI has placed the draft amendment in the public domain to seek feedback from stakeholders. Objections and suggestions can be submitted within 60 days of the date on which copies of the Official Gazette carrying the notification are made available to the public. The food regulator will review the submissions received within the stipulated timeframe before taking up the amendment for finalisation. FSSAI’s new pesticide residue limits for tea: What consumers and industry need to know
FSSAI has proposed maximum residue limits (MRLs) of 20 ppm for acetamiprid and 50 ppm for imidacloprid in tea, with the draft regulations open for stakeholder consultation
Timsy Jaipuria
18 Oct 2026 3:45 PM IST
Click the Play button to hear this message in audio format
The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) has proposed new maximum residue limits (MRLs) for two pesticides – acetamiprid and imidacloprid – in tea, marking another step in the country's ongoing review of food safety standards. The proposed limits are intended to provide clearer regulatory benchmarks for pesticide residues and strengthen monitoring across the tea supply chain.
Under the draft Food Safety and Standards (Contaminants, Toxins and Residues) Amendment Regulations, 2026, published in the Gazette of India on October 16, FSSAI has proposed an MRL of 20 milligrams per kilogram (mg/kg), or parts per million (ppm), for acetamiprid and 50 mg/kg for imidacloprid in tea. The draft regulations are open to stakeholder consultation and are subject to finalisation.
For consumers, the key distinction is that these are proposed regulatory limits, not finalised standards. An MRL specifies the maximum legally permitted pesticide residue concentration in a food commodity. It does not, by itself, indicate the amount of pesticide a person consumes in a cup of tea or establish the health risk from a particular residue level.
How India's proposed limits compare internationally
The proposed acetamiprid limit of 20 ppm is lower than the corresponding limits of 30 ppm in Japan and 50 ppm in the United States, according to the information accompanying the proposal. The proposed imidacloprid limit has been framed with reference to international Codex standards.
Also Read:
FSSAI proposes ban on sucrose, fructose in foods for babies up to 6 months: What parents need to know
Such comparisons provide context for India's regulatory approach, but they should be interpreted carefully. Different countries may set residue limits based on crop-specific agricultural practices, authorised pesticide uses, residue studies and regulatory assessments. A lower MRL does not automatically mean that a country's tea is safer, just as a higher limit does not necessarily mean that a product poses a health risk.
The significance of the proposed Indian standards will depend on the scientific evidence underpinning them, the applicable enforcement framework and the final regulations notified by the food safety authority.
What does this mean for tea drinkers?
For households, tea remains a widely consumed everyday product, making effective residue monitoring an important part of food safety oversight. Clearly defined limits can help food businesses and enforcement agencies assess compliance and identify products that do not meet prescribed standards.
Also Read:
FSSAI orders Everest to recall cumin powder from market after sample found ‘unsafe’
However, consumers should not interpret the proposal as evidence that tea currently available in the market is unsafe. Nor does the announcement establish that all tea products contain either pesticide. Actual residue levels vary depending on cultivation practices, pesticide application, processing and other factors.
Consumers can continue to make informed purchasing decisions by choosing products from reputable manufacturers, checking packaging and following official food safety advisories. The draft proposal does not, on its own, warrant a change in normal tea-drinking habits.
Implications for growers and the tea industry
For tea growers, processors, exporters and testing laboratories, the proposed limits could provide greater clarity on compliance requirements once the rules are finalised. The industry may need to assess pesticide-use practices, testing protocols and supply-chain controls against the eventual standards.
Pesticides play a role in managing crop pests and limiting agricultural losses. Regulation therefore involves balancing effective pest management with the need to protect consumers and ensure compliance with food safety requirements. Farmers may require appropriate guidance on authorised pesticide use, application practices and residue management to meet evolving standards without unnecessarily increasing production costs.
The proposal also forms part of a broader regulatory review. Earlier measures included the delisting of 13 pesticides identified as having higher toxicity, according to the information accompanying the announcement.

FSSAI initiates prosecution against Surya Food & Agro for using cattle feed bran in Priyagold biscuits production
The regulator has also initiated prosecution proceedings against Dodla Dairy and UEIR Organic Foods over food safety violations involving substandard full cream milk and pesticide residues in yellow raisins, respectively

The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) has initiated legal proceedings for prosecution against Surya Food & Agro, the manufacturer of Priyagold biscuits, for allegedly using cattle feed bran in biscuit production and violating food safety requirements.
The regulator has also initiated prosecution proceedings against
Dodla Dairy
and UEIR Organic Foods over food safety violations involving substandard full cream milk and pesticide residues in yellow raisins, respectively.
The
FSSAI
said that it has "initiated legal proceedings for prosecution" against these three companies for "serious food safety violations".
The actions follow regulatory inspections and laboratory analysis that identified non-compliance with food safety standards. The proceedings have been initiated under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006.

Freedom Rice Bran Oil: Why FSSAI issued notices to BigBasket, Flipkart
Cattle feed bran found at Priyagold biscuit manufacturer's facility
FSSAI inspected Surya Food & Agro following a
consumer
complaint and found serious deficiencies related to food safety, hygiene and manufacturing practices.
During the inspection, the regulator found that the company was using bran intended for cattle feed in the manufacture of Priyagold biscuits. The gunny bags containing the material were marked to indicate that it was meant for cattle consumption.
The inspection also identified shortcomings in several areas, including plant hygiene, pest control, raw material storage and segregation, personnel hygiene, maintenance of the premises and handling of intermediate formulations.
"Bran meant for cattle feed and not intended for human consumption, was found being used as a raw material in Priyagold biscuit manufacturing as a source of fibre," the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) said in a social media post on Saturday.
These findings raised concerns about the company's compliance with prescribed food safety and hygiene requirements.
FSSAI
had earlier suspended Surya Food & Agro's licence following serious non-compliances detected during the inspection. The regulator has now initiated legal proceedings for prosecution against the company over the violations.
Dodla Dairy's full cream milk sample found substandard
FSSAI has also initiated prosecution proceedings against Dodla Dairy after a regulatory sample of its full cream milk was declared substandard.
The sample was collected by the food safety authorities and sent for laboratory analysis. The Food Analyst found that the milk did not conform to the prescribed specifications for milk fat.
Upon appeal by the company, the sample was referred to the Referral Food Laboratory, which "confirmed that the sample was unsafe due to the presence of detergent/caustic soda and substandard due to milk fat below the minimum prescribed limit."
The laboratory findings established violations relating to substandard food under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006.
Following the analysis, the competent authority granted sanction for initiating prosecution against Dodla Dairy and other concerned food business operators associated with the manufacture and marketing of the product.
The authorities have directed further prosecution proceedings in connection with the substandard food findings.

In a separate case, FSSAI initiated legal proceedings for prosecution against UEIR Organic Foods after pesticide residues were detected in a sample of yellow raisins sold by the company.

The cases involving Surya Food & Agro, Dodla Dairy and UEIR Organic Foods highlight separate instances of alleged non-compliance with food safety requirements, ranging from the use of an ingredient designated for animal feed to milk
quality
deficiencies and pesticide contamination.
The prosecution proceedings mark a further step in the regulator's response to the violations identified through consumer complaints, inspections and laboratory testing. The cases will proceed through the applicable legal process under food safety regulations.

FSSAI acts against Radisson Blu, e-commerce platforms over safety lapses
Food regulator flags hygiene violations at Radisson Blu, misleading claims for rice bran oil on e-commerce platforms, and suspends or cancels licences of two food businesses
Ananya Podder
New Delhi
4 min read
Last Updated :
Oct 16 2026 | 6:05 PM
IST
Listen to This Article
The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) has taken action against a hotel, three food businesses and two e-commerce platforms for food safety non-compliance and misleading claims, the regulator said in social media posts on Friday.
The action covers AB Hotels Limited (Radisson Blu Hotel), DNV Food Products Limited, Jhanvitanni, Gemini Edibles and Fats India Limited, and e-commerce platforms BigBasket and Flipkart India.
The regulator further issued an improvement notice to Radisson Blu Hotel over poor maintenance of premises and equipment, such as rusted machinery, freezer leakage and deficiencies in refrigeration, temperature monitoring, ventilation, flooring and lighting.
“Inadequate cleaning and sanitisation, stagnant water, drainage and food-waste issues, and deficiencies in pest control were observed, including cockroach and fly activity,” it said. “Food procurement and receiving checks were inadequate, including receipt of fungal-affected and deteriorated fruits and vegetables, with deficiencies in approved-vendor records and traceability.”
Cooking oil suitability checks were not carried out as required, and oils with TPC (total polar compounds) values of 31 and 24.4 were found in use in the NYC Kitchen, said the regulator. There was improper segregation of raw and cooked foods, vegetarian and non-vegetarian items, allergenic and non-allergenic foods, and food and non-food items. Food handlers were found working without gloves and hairnets, wearing jewellery and with long nails.

The FSSAI licence was not prominently displayed either. The FBO (food business operator) has been directed to take immediate corrective measures and submit a detailed action taken report (ATR), with supporting documentary and photographic evidence. Failure to comply may lead to the suspension of the FSSAI licence, according to the regulator.
FSSAI also issued a notice to Gemini Edibles and Fats India Limited, Innovative Retail Concepts Private Limited (BigBasket) and Flipkart India over misleading claims for “Freedom Cooking Rice Bran Oil.”
According to the regulator, the product was promoted on e-commerce platforms and social media with claims such as “Reduces bad cholesterol and maintains/increases good cholesterol” and “10,000+ PPM Natural Oryzanol,” linking its consumption to cholesterol management and heart health.
FSSAI found that these claims are not covered or permitted for edible vegetable oil (rice bran oil) under the Advertising and Claims Regulations, 2018. It also noted that Gemini Edibles and Fats India Limited was offering food products through its own e-commerce website without appearing to hold a valid central licence covering e-commerce activity.
The FBOs have been directed to show cause why action should not be initiated under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, and the rules and regulations made under it.
DNV Food Products Limited had its licence suspended after FSSAI said it had observed food being manufactured and stored amid inadequate cleaning, stagnant water, cobwebs and flies, including a fly in direct contact with papad. Food handlers were found not wearing gloves and masks. Processing equipment was rusted, while flooring was damaged, walls were damp, paint was flaking, and ventilation and lighting were inadequate.
Products were processed and repacked without the required licence endorsement, and food-grade packaging certificates, migration reports and mock recall records were unavailable, according to the regulator.
FSSAI also cancelled the licence of Jhanvitanni after continued non-compliance with food safety requirements and operation despite licence suspension, it said. Severe hygiene and sanitation deficiencies were observed at the premises.
Corrective actions submitted by the FBO were found unsatisfactory, said FSSAI, with several previously identified non-compliances remaining unaddressed. The FBO also failed to comply with hygiene, sanitation and Food Safety Management System (FSMS) requirements, including the requirement for a third-party audit (TPA), despite repeated directions and regulatory action.

news_title: FSSAI proposes ban on sucrose, fructose in foods for babies up to 6 months: What parents need to know - The Federal

Health
FSSAI proposes ban on sucrose, fructose in foods for babies up to 6 months: What parents need to know
FSSAI has invited objections and suggestions from stakeholders within 60 days from the date on which copies of the Official Gazette containing the notification are made available to the public.
Timsy Jaipuria
17 Oct 2026 3:48 PM IST
Parents buying infant nutrition products may see tighter safeguards on added sugars if a proposed food safety amendment takes effect, with the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) seeking to prohibit the addition of sucrose and fructose in products intended for babies up to six months of age.
The food regulator has published a draft amendment to the Food Safety and Standards (Foods for Infant Nutrition) Regulations, 2020, in the Gazette of India on October 16. The proposal would prohibit manufacturers from adding sucrose and fructose to infant nutrition products meant for this age group, strengthening existing rules that allow these sugars under specified conditions.
For consumers, the move could mean stricter controls over how infant nutrition products are formulated, with a greater emphasis on age-appropriate carbohydrate sources. However, the proposal is still at the draft stage and is not yet a final regulatory requirement.
What changes for parents?
Under the existing regulations, lactose and glucose polymers are the preferred carbohydrate sources in infant nutrition products. Sucrose and fructose may currently be added when needed as a carbohydrate source, subject to a combined limit of 20 per cent of total carbohydrates.
Also read:
Drug price controls: Protecting patients without distorting the market
The proposed amendment would remove this allowance for products intended for infants up to six months of age. If finalised, manufacturers would have to reformulate products in this category to comply with the new restriction.
For parents, the key takeaway is that the proposed change concerns the ingredients manufacturers may add to infant nutrition products. It does not mean that all carbohydrates will be prohibited, nor does it establish that every product currently on the market contains added sucrose or fructose.
Why does it matter for infant health?
The first six months are a critical period for infant growth and development, when feeding choices and nutritional adequacy are particularly important. Reducing the scope for adding sucrose and fructose to products for this age group is intended to strengthen safeguards against unnecessary exposure to these sugars.
The broader public health concern is that early dietary exposure to added sugars can contribute to the development of taste preferences for sweet foods and may form part of dietary patterns associated with future health risks. However, the proposed amendment itself does not establish that removing these ingredients will, on its own, prevent childhood obesity or other health conditions.
Also read:
What cheaper cancer drugs, tighter ad rules mean for patients and the pharma industry
The proposal also aligns with established infant-feeding guidance that recommends exclusive breastfeeding for the first six months of life, where possible. Infant formula and other appropriate products remain important considerations when breastfeeding is not possible or when an infant needs an alternative under appropriate medical guidance.
Will infant formula prices or product choices change?
The immediate impact on consumers is uncertain. If the amendment is finalised, manufacturers may need to review ingredient sourcing, formulations, production processes and product labelling to ensure compliance.
Whether these changes affect retail prices, product availability or the range of formulations offered will depend on how manufacturers respond and how the final rules are framed. The draft notification does not announce a price change, a product recall or an immediate withdrawal of existing products.
Parents should therefore not assume that products currently available are automatically unsafe or that they need to switch products in anticipation of the proposal. Any feeding changes for young infants should be made with appropriate medical advice.
What happens next?
FSSAI has invited objections and suggestions from stakeholders within 60 days from the date on which copies of the Official Gazette containing the notification are made available to the public. The regulator will consider submissions before finalising the amendment.
Until the proposal is finalised and comes into force, the existing regulatory provisions continue to apply. For consumers, the significance of the move lies in the direction of regulation: tighter controls on the formulation of foods for the youngest infants, with a focus on nutritional suitability…[truncated]

efet_body:
Maharashtra FDA bans loose spice powder sales, orders Statewide crackdown on adulteration
The Food Safety Commissioner’s order bans prohibited colouring agents, including Metanil Yellow and Rhodamine B, and adulterants such as brick powder and chalk, and requires all spice powders to be packed and sealed at the place of production before sale
Updated
- October 18, 2026 02:25 am IST - Mumbai
Yohaan Varghese
READ LATER
SEE ALL
Remove
Manufacturers have been directed to maintain clean, dry and pest-free premises, with drying spices on public roads, near drains, garbage bins or cattle sheds strictly prohibited. Image for the purpose of representation only.
| Photo Credit: File
The Maharashtra Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has prohibited the sale of loose, unpackaged spice powders and mixed spices across the State as part of a crackdown on adulteration, unhygienic manufacturing practices and misleading labelling. The order, issued by Food Safety Commissioner Tukaram Mundhe on Thursday (October 15, 2026) mandates stricter safety standards across the spice supply chain, from manufacturing to retail sale.
The directive covers manufacturers, wholesalers, retailers, e-commerce operators, hotels, restaurants and caterers dealing in spices, including turmeric, chilli, coriander, cumin, black pepper and mixed spice products. All spice powders and mixed spices must be packed and sealed at the place of production before distribution or sale.
The FDA has banned the use of prohibited colouring agents, including Metanil Yellow, Rhodamine B, Sudan dyes and Lead Chromate, along with adulterants such as brick powder, chalk, sawdust, and foreign starch. The sale of inferior-quality spices and spices from which extracts have been removed is also prohibited.
The order further prohibits the use of ethylene oxide for sterilising spices, citing its potential carcinogenic effects. Spices will be tested for pesticide residues, aflatoxins, heavy metals, and other contaminants.
Manufacturers have been directed to maintain clean, dry and pest-free premises, with drying spices on public roads, near drains, garbage bins or cattle sheds strictly prohibited. All operators must possess valid FSSAI licences or registrations, as a trade licence alone will not authorise spice manufacturing or grinding.
Packaged spices must carry mandatory information, including ingredients, manufacturer details, FSSAI licence number, batch number and manufacturing and expiry dates. Unsubstantiated claims regarding purity, organic production or health benefits will attract action.
Action to extend beyond retailers
In cases of adulteration, the FDA will trace the source of contamination and investigate manufacturers, grinding units, repackaging businesses and suppliers of prohibited substances, rather than restricting action to retailers.
Officials will examine purchase records, production details and batch numbers to identify violations. Depending on their severity, action may include seizure of products, market recalls, suspension or cancellation of licences and prosecution.
Under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, selling substandard food can attract fines of up to ₹5 lakh, while misleading advertisements can result in penalties of up to ₹10 lakh. Cases where unsafe food causes death can attract imprisonment ranging from seven years to life, along with a minimum fine of ₹10 lakh.
The FDA has directed food safety officers across Maharashtra to conduct compliance inspections and submit monthly enforcement reports. Designated Officers must report to Divisional Joint Commissioners by the third of every month, while consolidated reports must reach the Commissioner’s office by the fifth.
Consumers can report suspected adulteration, unhygienic production or misleading labelling through the FDA’s toll-free helpline, 1800 222 365, or its online grievance portal at complaints.mahafda.in.

FSSAI said these claims were not covered under the applicable Advertising and Claims Regulations, 2018. It also flagged the absence of an apparent valid Central Licence for Gemini Edibles' e-commerce activities.
The concerned businesses have been directed to show cause why action should not be initiated under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, and related rules.
